implementation_notes: queue.Queue is a multi-producer, multi-consumer queue whose get() removes an item for exactly one caller, so N daemon-free worker threads looping `item = q.get()` implement the competing-consumer pool directly, with q.task_done()/q.join() for shutdown and maxsize for backpressure. Nothing of the classic structure remains to write - the queue is the arbiter - and the honest limits are elsewhere: threads share the GIL (good for I/O-bound handlers, poor for CPU-bound ones) and the queue dies with the process.
pitfalls: The GIL means threads add no CPU parallelism: CPU-bound handlers need ProcessPoolExecutor/multiprocessing or a process-based worker (Celery) instead.
Forgetting q.task_done() (or swallowing exceptions before it) hangs q.join() at shutdown and hides poison messages.
A queue.Queue with maxsize=0 is unbounded - overload becomes memory growth rather than producer backpressure.

variants.name: asyncio.Queue + N worker tasks (single event loop)
variants.idiom_name: asyncio.Queue + N worker tasks (single event loop)
variants.implementation_notes: The async form replaces threads with tasks: asyncio.Queue hands each item to exactly one awaiting `await q.get()` coroutine, so N worker tasks compete inside one event loop and thousands of concurrent I/O operations are possible with a handful of workers. What changes versus threads is discipline, not semantics - every handler must stay non-blocking (run_in_executor for sync work) or it stalls the whole pool - and the queue lives in one process/event loop, so multi-core scaling still needs processes or a broker.
variants.code_sketch:
import asyncio

async def worker(q):
    while True:
        item = await q.get()
        try: await process(item)     # never block the loop here
        finally: q.task_done()

async def main():
    q = asyncio.Queue(maxsize=100)
    workers = [asyncio.create_task(worker(q)) for _ in range(n)]
    ...  # producer: await q.put(job); await q.join(); cancel workers
pitfalls: A blocking call (requests, time.sleep, heavy CPU work) inside a worker freezes every other worker in the loop; use aiohttp/asyncio.sleep and executor offloads.
Task exceptions are swallowed until awaited: a worker that dies from an exception silently shrinks the pool - collect and supervise the worker tasks.
The queue is process-local; asyncio alone gives no cross-process or durable competition - that is a broker's job.

variants.name: Broker-backed worker processes (Celery/RQ/SQS consumers)
variants.implementation_notes: The deployment form used when availability matters: N worker processes pull from a real durable queue (Celery on Redis/RabbitMQ, RQ, an SQS or Kafka consumer), so competition survives process restarts and spans hosts, and the broker - not an in-process queue - owns acknowledgement and redelivery. The Python code shrinks to the task function; pool size, concurrency and prefetch are deployment settings, and the interesting work moves to idempotency, retry policy and dead-letter configuration.
pitfalls: acks_late=True is required for at-least-once processing, but it makes duplicate delivery normal - tasks must be idempotent.
Prefetch settings let one worker reserve many messages; a long task then starves sibling workers on the same queue.
An unhandled exception moves the task to retries/failure; without max_retries and a dead-letter path a poison task retries forever.
